question: Is there a significant upward trend in world % stocks overexploited?
evidence: Hamed-Rao MK p < 0.001, Sen +0.55 pp/yr [0.50, 0.59]; assessment years only p < 0.001; SAU world p < 0.001
note: No slowdown after 2015: slope change -0.15 pp/yr (p = 0.489), Chow p = 0.892

question: Does global catch cross-correlate with % stocks overexploited at some lag?
evidence: Largest |r| on stationary series: r = -0.23 at lag 4 (Holm p = 1.000); prewhitened min Holm p = 1.000; Granger min Holm p = 1.000; cointegration p = 0.199
note: Catch plateaued since the 1990s while overexploitation kept rising: no short-run or long-run link in this data. Catch is a weak proxy for fishing pressure (caveat 1).

question: Is there a significant worsening trend in SEA (rising % overexploited or falling MTL)?
evidence: SEA % overexploited MK p < 0.001, Sen +7.4 pp/decade; 16/16 countries+EEZs rising after Holm; FAO Area 71 p = 0.074
note: MTL ('fishing down') falls significantly 1990–2019 only in: Philippines; SEA-wide MTL rises, so the worsening shows in stock status rather than trophic level

question: Does SEA catch cross-correlate with mean trophic level at some lag?
evidence: Smallest raw p: Philippines lag 9, r = -0.31 (p = 0.016, Holm within unit p = 0.180); 0 of 66 lag tests significant after Holm
note: Stock status is not used as the response: Sea Around Us derives it from catch (circular)

question: Is the SEA trend in % overexploited significantly worse than the world trend?
evidence: SAU 1990–2019: SEA +0.97 vs world +0.97 pp/yr, difference -0.00 [-0.09, +0.08], p = 0.911; countries worse (Holm): Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand; better: Vietnam
decision: Fail to reject H0 for SEA as a whole; reject for Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand
note: 1950–2019 difference -0.05 pp/yr (p = 0.002). FAO Area 71 vs world +1.03 pp/yr (p = 0.027), but without the 2021 jump p = 0.084. SEA MTL rises 0.0021/yr slower than the world's (p = 0.001)

question: Is catch per unit effort falling (more effort for the same fish)?
evidence: World CPUE -35% 1990–94 → 2013–17 (catch -6%, effort +44%), Sen -1.9%/yr, p < 0.001; SEA -50% (Sen -3.6%/yr, p < 0.001); falling significantly in Malaysia, Indonesia, Philippines
note: Not a hypothesis from the plan; supports the depletion explanation for flat catch + rising overexploitation

question: Does world fishing effort cross-correlate with % stocks overexploited at some lag?
evidence: Largest effect r = +0.35 at lag 3 (raw p = 0.026, Holm p = 0.291); SAU min Holm p = 0.266; Granger min Holm p = 0.072; cointegration with FAO p = 0.078
note: Short-run (year-to-year) changes in effort do not line up with changes in stock status; the long-run level link is weak (cointegration p = 0.078, 10% level only). See CPUE for the long-run story.

question: Does SEA fishing effort cross-correlate with % overexploited or mean trophic level at some lag?
evidence: 1 of 132 lag tests significant after Holm within unit: Indonesia Δ MTL lag 0 r = +0.35 (Holm p = 0.043); across all 132 tests min Holm p = 0.517
decision: Weak: reject H0 only for Indonesia Δ MTL at lag 0 (r = +0.35); not significant once all 132 tests are corrected together
note: Stock status can be tested here (effort is independent of SAU's catch-based status). Thailand's effort series stays non-stationary (source breaks), so its lags are unreliable.

question: Does ocean warming correlate with world % stocks overexploited beyond their shared upward trend?
evidence: Levels ρ = +0.86; after removing linear trends ρ = -0.11 with FAO (p = 0.450) but +0.44 with SAU (p < 0.001); cointegration with constant p = 0.051 (FAO), = 0.033 (SAU), with trend p = 0.359 (FAO; ocean heat content = 0.038), jointly with effort p = 0.193; CCF min Holm p = 0.563; Granger min Holm p = 1.000
decision: Fail to reject H0 (shared trend only; no consistent link beyond it)
note: Warming and overexploitation share an upward trend; beyond it the two sources disagree in sign (the SAU series is S-shaped, so a straight-line detrend leaves curvature that matches accelerating warming) and no year-to-year link exists. The data cannot separate warming from other steadily rising drivers.

question: Do changes in SEA sea temperature cross-correlate with % overexploited, mean trophic level or catch?
evidence: SEA SST +0.12 °C/decade (MK p < 0.001); 2 of 198 lag tests significant after Holm within unit and response: SEA Δ % overexploited lag 10 r = +0.44 (Holm p = 0.006); Indonesia Δ MTL lag 4 r = +0.36 (Holm p = 0.032); across all 198 tests min Holm p = 0.110
decision: Weak: 2 isolated lag(s) significant within unit; none across all 198 tests
note: Significant lags sit at the edge of the tested range or in a single country and vanish under the all-test correction, so they are treated as chance findings unless replicated.

question: Do shipping volume, dam building or aquaculture growth track world % stocks overexploited beyond their shared upward trend?
evidence: Levels ρ +0.93 to +1.00; linear-detrended ρ significant after Holm in Container port traffic × SAU (+0.85, quadratic +0.38), Seaborne trade volume × SAU (+0.65, quadratic +0.29), Dams completed (cumulative) × FAO (+0.56, quadratic +0.56), Dams completed (cumulative) × SAU (-0.90, quadratic -0.65); consistent in both sources and both detrends: none; cointegration: Dams completed (cumulative) × FAO c p = 0.191; Dams completed (cumulative) × FAO ct p = 0.062; Dams completed (cumulative) × SAU c p = 0.652; Dams completed (cumulative) × SAU ct p = 0.955; Aquaculture production × FAO c p = 0.175; Aquaculture production × FAO ct p = 0.330; Aquaculture production × SAU c p = 0.554; Aquaculture production × SAU ct p = 0.494; CCF 0 of 74 lag tests significant across all (min Holm p = 0.299)
decision: Fail to reject H0 (shared trend only; no consistent link beyond it)
note: 4 of 4 linear-detrended links either lose significance under a quadratic detrend, have no significant counterpart in the other source, or flip sign between FAO and SAU (dams): they reflect curvature, not co-movement. Shipping starts in 2000 (≤ 22 overlapping years), so its power is low; GDAT completions are a lower bound that thins after ~2005 (database lag).

question: Do changes in SEA port traffic, seaborne trade, liner connectivity, dam building or aquaculture cross-correlate with % overexploited or mean trophic level?
evidence: 2 of 492 lag tests (60 unit × driver × response rows) significant after Holm within row: Thailand Dams completed (cumulative) -> Δ MTL lag 6 r = +0.46; Thailand Dams completed (cumulative) -> Δ MTL lag 7 r = +0.41; across all tests 0 (min Holm p = 0.480); SEA linear-detrended ρ with % overexploited significant after Holm for Dams completed (cumulative) (-0.59, quadratic +0.63), Aquaculture production (+0.65, quadratic +0.22); consistent under both detrends: none
decision: Weak: 2 isolated lag(s) significant within row; none across all 492 tests
note: Shipping overlaps the SAU series for 19 changes only (2001–2019), so only strong links could be detected. Linear-detrended links that flip sign under a quadratic detrend are curvature artefacts.

question: Did % overexploited, mean trophic level or catch in the EEZs facing the Spratly Islands change after China's 2013–2016 island building, relative to other SEA EEZs?
evidence: DiD 2004–2019, event 2014, 4 treated vs 5 control EEZs: % overexploited β = +0.700 (randomization p = 0.913, Holm = 1.000); mean trophic level β = -0.030 (randomization p = 0.476, Holm = 1.000); log catch β = -0.083 (randomization p = 0.587, Holm = 1.000); edge EEZs as treated: % overexploited β = +1.51 (p = 0.701); placebo 2009: β = -8.04 (p = 0.286)
decision: Fail to reject H0 (no post-2014 change specific to Spratly-facing EEZs)
note: Island building is a single dated event; military outposts were built on the same features in 2014–2018, so the two cannot be separated. Vietnam's own reclamation (2022–2025) is after the fisheries data end (2019). Only 9 EEZs → randomization inference (126 assignments) instead of clustered errors.

question: Pooling all EEZs (fixed effects absorb the common trend): does a pressure measure raise % overexploited or lower mean trophic level?
evidence: 0 of 36 coefficients significant after Holm (wild cluster bootstrap); robust to unit trends and in the 'worse' direction: none; smallest raw p: foreign-fleet share of catch (%) → % overexploited (same year, EEZ/country + year FE), standardised β = -0.38, raw p = 0.020, Holm p = 0.727
note: Catch is tested only against mean trophic level (SAU stock status is derived from catch). Effort uses the 5-country panel (1950–2017; break-adjusted), the rest the 11-EEZ panel (1950–2019). Few clusters → wild cluster bootstrap p-values (Webb weights).

question: Has the share of rebuilding stocks increased since the SDGs were adopted (2015)?
evidence: EEZ-level 2015–19 vs 2010–14: 6 of 11 EEZs higher, median change +0.07 pp, one-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.260; SEA slope change after 2015 -0.43 pp/yr (p = 0.002); world +1.00 pp/yr (p = 0.016); SEA level 9.0% → 9.3%
decision: Mixed: world rebuilding accelerated after 2015, SEA's did not
note: Sea Around Us labels a stock 'rebuilding' when its catch recovers after a collapse (catch-based, Kleisner et al. 2013). The 'restore stocks' half of SDG 14.4 is judged on this measure only. Country slope changes after 2015 (Holm): Malaysia -0.28 pp/yr (p = 0.244); Indonesia +0.30 pp/yr (p = 0.288); Thailand +1.66 pp/yr (p < 0.001); Vietnam -1.18 pp/yr (p = 0.002); Philippines -2.64 pp/yr (p = 0.001)

question: Since 1990, has the Fishing-in-Balance index fallen (catch no longer compensating for trophic-level change)?
evidence: SEA FiB Sen +0.15/decade (MK p < 0.001); world +0.05/decade (p = 0.014); 1990–94 → 2015–19 SEA change +0.39 = catch +0.32 + trophic level +0.07; falling after Holm in: Thailand, Thailand – Gulf of Thailand; rising in: Indonesia, Vietnam, Malaysia – Peninsula West, Indonesia – Central, Indonesia – Eastern, Vietnam (EEZ)
decision: Fail to reject H0 for SEA (FiB not falling); falling in Thailand, Thailand – Gulf of Thailand
note: FiB > 0 and rising means catches grew faster than a trophic-level change alone would allow, usually through expansion (new grounds, offshore/pelagic stocks); FiB falling means the ecosystem no longer delivers. TE = 0.1 by convention.

question: On current trends, will the share of overexploited stocks in 2030 be higher than its latest value?
evidence: World (FAO, linear): 35.5% in 2021 → 41.3% in 2030 [95% PI 36.7–46.1]; SEA (SAU, ets): 43.9% → 53.5% [49.2–57.8]; world 2030 lower bound above 35.5% in 2 of 3 models (linear 36.7, ets 34.7, arima(2, 1, 1) 36.7); rise with 95% confidence AND trend validated in the back-test: World (FAO); a no-change forecast beat every trend model in: World (SAU), SEA (SAU), Malaysia (SAU), Indonesia (SAU), Thailand (SAU)
note: Model per series chosen by a 5-year back-test (linear trend on logit, damped-trend ETS, ARIMA with drift); the logit keeps forecasts within 0–100%. A forecast extends past trends, so it assumes no change in management; it shows the distance from the SDG target, not a prediction of policy. Where the no-change forecast wins the back-test (most Sea Around Us series flattened in 2015–19), the projected rise is not supported and the honest reading is 'no improvement', not 'further rise'.

question: Do two drivers TOGETHER explain world % overexploited beyond the shared trend, even if neither does alone?
evidence: 28 pairs × 2 sources, joint HAC F-test, Holm within specification. Year-to-year changes: 10 of 56 significant (FAO 0, SAU 10): Catch (FAO capture) + Container port traffic (SAU, n = 19) Holm p = 0.009; Catch (FAO capture) + Seaborne trade volume (SAU, n = 19) Holm p = 0.012; Fishing effort (nominal) + Container port traffic (SAU, n = 17) Holm p = 0.038; Sea-surface temperature + Container port traffic (SAU, n = 19) Holm p = 0.005; Sea-surface temperature + Seaborne trade volume (SAU, n = 19) Holm p < 0.001; Ocean heat content + Container port traffic (SAU, n = 19) Holm p = 0.046; Container port traffic + Seaborne trade volume (SAU, n = 19) Holm p = 0.030; Container port traffic + Dams completed (cumulative) (SAU, n = 19) Holm p = 0.016; Container port traffic + Aquaculture production (SAU, n = 19) Holm p = 0.014; Seaborne trade volume + Dams completed (cumulative) (SAU, n = 19) Holm p = 0.033. Levels with linear/quadratic trend: 51 of 112 F-tests significant, but only 4 pass the cointegration check (the rest are spurious regressions; signs flip between specifications). Significant only as a pair (neither driver alone): 1. Supported in both sources: none
decision: Weak: 14 pair test(s) significant, but none supported in both data sources
note: Shipping series start in 2000, so their pairs use about 20 years. Volumes enter as Δlog (growth), indices as first differences. Levels results need Engle-Granger cointegration (MacKinnon p, Holm) to count.

question: Does one pressure change the effect of another on % overexploited or mean trophic level (interaction in a country panel with fixed effects)?
evidence: 4 pre-chosen pairs × 2 responses × 2 specifications; 0 of 16 interaction terms significant after Holm (wild cluster bootstrap); robust to country trends: none; smallest raw p: Effort × sea temperature → mean trophic level (country + year FE) p = 0.046
note: 5 countries, 1960–2017. Drivers are centred before multiplying; both main effects and the fixed effects are partialled out (Frisch-Waugh-Lovell), and the interaction is tested with the wild cluster bootstrap (all 6^5 Webb draws).

question: Does any combination of the long-run drivers explain year-to-year changes in world % overexploited better than the trend (average change) alone, including on years the model has not seen?
evidence: FAO (1975–2017): BIC picks (trend only) (adds R² 0.00, HAC p n/a); all 6 drivers add R² 0.17 (HAC p = 0.013, circular-shift p = 0.229); LASSO keeps (none); held-out RMSE 1.60 pp (BIC subset) vs 1.45 pp (trend only); SAU (1961–2017): BIC picks Catch (FAO capture) (adds R² 0.10, HAC p = 0.009); all 6 drivers add R² 0.15 (HAC p = 0.021, circular-shift p = 0.469); LASSO keeps Catch (FAO capture); held-out RMSE 0.99 pp (BIC subset) vs 0.95 pp (trend only)
note: Year-to-year changes (levels regressions are spurious here, see H6a). Six drivers with series back to 1960 (shipping starts in 2000 and is left out). The BIC subset is re-chosen inside every training window, so the held-out comparison is free of selection bias. SAU stock status is derived from catch, so catch → SAU is partly circular.

question: Do nutrient (fertiliser) and pesticide run-off, plastic production, oil spills or ocean acidification track world % stocks overexploited beyond their shared trend?
evidence: Levels ρ -0.93 to +1.00 (oil spills fall while overexploitation rises); linear-detrended ρ significant after Holm in Nitrogen fertiliser per ha × FAO (+0.42, quadratic +0.26), Nitrogen fertiliser per ha × SAU (-0.80, quadratic -0.68), Plastic production × SAU (-0.89, quadratic -0.51); consistent under both detrends in one source only: Nitrogen fertiliser per ha × SAU (-0.80 / -0.68), Plastic production × SAU (-0.89 / -0.51); consistent in both sources and both detrends: none; cointegration p < 0.05 in 7 of 24 tests (Nitrogen fertiliser per ha × FAO c; Nitrogen fertiliser per ha × FAO ct; Pesticides per ha × FAO c; Pesticides per ha × FAO ct; Oil spills (number ≥ 7 t) × FAO c; Oil spills (number ≥ 7 t) × SAU c; Ocean acidity [H⁺] (Hawaii) × FAO c); CCF 0 of 130 lag tests significant across all (min Holm p = 0.396)
decision: Fail to reject H0 (shared trend only; no consistent link beyond it)
note: Pesticides and acidity start in 1990 (≤ 32 overlapping years). Acidity is measured at one open-ocean station (Hawaii) and stands for the global trend. Fertiliser and pesticides are applied on land; they measure the run-off pressure, not the concentration in the sea.

question: Do changes in SEA fertiliser and pesticide use or coastal chlorophyll-a (eutrophication) track % overexploited or mean trophic level, year to year or across countries?
evidence: CCF: 2 of 312 lag tests (36 unit × driver × response rows) significant within row: Indonesia Nitrogen fertiliser per ha -> Δ MTL lag 3 r = -0.38; Thailand Nitrogen fertiliser per ha -> Δ MTL lag 6 r = +0.47, 0 across all (min Holm p = 0.151); SEA detrended ρ with % overexploited consistent under both detrends: Pesticides per ha (ρ +0.44 linear, +0.45 quadratic, but it disappears without Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam). Panel (5 countries, country + year FE, wild bootstrap): 0 of 24 coefficients significant after Holm; robust to country trends in the 'worse' direction: none; smallest raw p: log pesticides per ha → mean trophic level (same year, country + year FE), standardised β +0.26, p = 0.049
decision: Weak: SEA-wide pesticides per ha link beyond the trend rests on Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam; 2 isolated lag(s) within row, none across all 312; 0 of 24 panel coefficients
note: Chlorophyll-a (SDG 14.1.1a) starts in 2005, so it overlaps the Sea Around Us series for 14 changes and 10 previous-5-year means only. Thailand's pesticide series drops by 90% in 2013 (a reporting break). SEA = mean of the 5 countries.

question: Does a pollution driver TOGETHER with another driver (or a second pollution driver) explain year-to-year changes in world % overexploited, in both data sources?
evidence: 63 pairs (6 pollution × 8 other drivers + 15 pollution pairs) × 2 sources, joint Newey-West F-test, Holm across all 126: FAO 1, SAU 6 (Ocean acidity [H⁺] (Hawaii) + Fishing effort (nominal) (FAO, n = 27) Holm p = 0.034; Pesticides per ha + Container port traffic (SAU, n = 19) Holm p = 0.028; Plastic production + Container port traffic (SAU, n = 19) Holm p = 0.026; Oil spilled (tonnes) + Container port traffic (SAU, n = 19) Holm p = 0.049; Oil spilled (tonnes) + Seaborne trade volume (SAU, n = 19) Holm p = 0.032; Ocean acidity [H⁺] (Hawaii) + Container port traffic (SAU, n = 19) Holm p = 0.027; Pesticides per ha + Oil spilled (tonnes) (SAU, n = 29) Holm p = 0.003); significant only as a pair (neither driver alone): 2; drivers significant alone: Container port traffic (SAU), Seaborne trade volume (SAU); supported in both sources: none
decision: Weak: 7 pair test(s) significant, but none supported in both data sources
note: Year-to-year changes only (iteration 6 showed levels-with-trend regressions are spurious here). Pairs with pesticides or acidity start in 1991 and pairs with shipping in 2001, so they use about 20–30 years.

question: Does nutrient or pesticide run-off change the effect of fishing effort, sea temperature or aquaculture on % overexploited or mean trophic level (SEA country panel)?
evidence: 4 pre-chosen pairs × 2 responses × 2 specifications; 0 of 16 interaction terms significant after Holm (wild cluster bootstrap); robust to country trends: none; smallest raw p: Fertiliser × aquaculture → mean trophic level (country + year FE) p = 0.046
note: 5 countries; fertiliser pairs 1961–2017, pesticide pair 1990–2017 (effort ends in 2017). Drivers centred before multiplying; main effects and fixed effects partialled out (Frisch-Waugh-Lovell); all 6^5 Webb draws enumerated.

hypothesis: H7e (iteration 7: best combination with pollution, world)
question: Does adding fertiliser, plastic and oil spills to the six long-run drivers give a combination that predicts year-to-year changes in world % overexploited better than the trend and than the best model without pollution, on years it has not seen?
evidence: FAO (1976–2017): BIC picks (trend only) (adds R² 0.00, HAC p n/a); the 3 pollution drivers add Shapley R² 0.03 (block p given the other 6 = 0.568); all 9 add R² 0.18 (circular-shift p = 0.647); LASSO keeps (none); held-out RMSE 1.66 pp with pollution vs 1.66 without vs 1.49 trend only; SAU (1971–2017): BIC picks Catch (FAO capture), Nitrogen fertiliser per ha (adds R² 0.17, HAC p = 0.042); the 3 pollution drivers add Shapley R² 0.16 (block p given the other 6 = 0.004); all 9 add R² 0.26 (circular-shift p = 0.351); LASSO keeps Catch (FAO capture), Nitrogen fertiliser per ha; held-out RMSE 1.01 pp with pollution vs 1.02 without vs 0.90 trend only
note: Year-to-year changes; 9 drivers → 512 subsets, BIC subset and LASSO λ re-chosen in every training window. The no-pollution comparison runs on the same years (the oil-spill series starts in 1970 and plastic has no 1974 value, so the years differ slightly from H6c).

hypothesis: H7f (iteration 7: coastal nutrient loading, SEA seas)
question: Where nitrogen or phosphorus loading to a Southeast Asian sea rises faster than in the other seas, do its stocks become more overexploited or its catch fall down the food web faster?
evidence: 5 large marine ecosystems (Bay of Bengal, Gulf of Thailand, South China Sea, Sulu-Celebes, Indonesian Sea), Sea Around Us; 2 nutrients × 2 responses × lag 0/1 × 2 specifications; 0 of 16 significant after Holm (wild cluster bootstrap); significant in both specifications with the same sign: 0; smallest raw p (changes): Nitrogen loading → mean trophic level lag 0 β_std +0.26, p = 0.075
note: Loading is modelled (Global NEWS 2 via OWID), 2000–2015; nitrogen is constant after 2010 in the source, so nitrogen tests use 2001–2010 only (phosphorus 2001–2015). 5 clusters: all 6^5 Webb draws enumerated. Fixed effects absorb each sea's level and the shocks shared by all 5 seas, so only differences between seas are tested.

question: Across assessed stocks, does fishing above the sustainable level (U/Umsy > 1) in one year predict that the stock shrinks relative to Bmsy the next year?
evidence: RAM Legacy v4.66, 432 stocks, 21157 stock-years, stock + year fixed effects, SE clustered by stock: β = -0.030 (p < 0.001): doubling U/Umsy shrinks B/Bmsy by 2.1% the next year; lags 1–3 sum -0.028 (p < 0.001); ≥ 30-year stocks -0.029 (p < 0.001); 1980+ -0.057 (p < 0.001). Reverse direction (management response): low B/Bmsy is followed by a cut in U/Umsy, β = +0.055 (p < 0.001). 248 stocks fell below Bmsy after ≥ 3 years above it; in the 3 years before, median U/Umsy = 1.28
note: Assessment outputs, not independent measurements: B and U come from the same stock-assessment model, so part of the link is built into how assessments are made. Coverage is mostly the US, Japan, New Zealand, Chile, Canada, Australia and Europe; only 3 stocks (two tunas, blue shark) touch SEA waters, so this is a global mechanism result, not a SEA one. Lagged dependent variable with fixed effects (Nickell bias) is small with ~50 years per stock.

hypothesis: H8b (iteration 8: crackdowns on foreign/illegal fishing, SEA)
question: After Indonesia's 2014 foreign-vessel moratorium and Thailand's 2015 IUU reforms, did their EEZs end up with fewer overexploited stocks or a higher trophic level than the other SEA EEZs?
evidence: DiD 2008–2019, event 2015 (randomization inference: Indonesia 3 of 11 EEZs, Thailand 2 of 8). First stage: Indonesia foreign share of catch (%) β -1.39 (p = 0.430); Indonesia log catch β +0.26 (p = 0.042); Thailand foreign share of catch (%) β +1.29 (p = 0.464); Thailand log catch β -0.18 (p = 0.179). Outcomes: Indonesia % overexploited β -3.23 (p = 0.497); Indonesia mean trophic level β -0.00 (p = 0.903); Thailand % overexploited β -0.35 (p = 0.964); Thailand mean trophic level β +0.06 (p = 0.071); Holm over 2 outcomes per policy; placebos (fake 2011 event): Indonesia placebo: fake event 2011 % overexploited β -0.12 (p = 1.000); Indonesia placebo: fake event 2011 mean trophic level β +0.02 (p = 0.576); Thailand placebo: fake event 2011 % overexploited β +3.84 (p = 0.429); Thailand placebo: fake event 2011 mean trophic level β +0.01 (p = 0.786); exploratory, not in the verdict (post = 2017–19, chosen after seeing the event study): Indonesia exploratory: post = 2017–2019 % overexploited β -3.56 (p = 0.485); Indonesia exploratory: post = 2017–2019 mean trophic level β -0.00 (p = 0.885); Thailand exploratory: post = 2017–2019 % overexploited β -3.97 (p = 0.500); Thailand exploratory: post = 2017–2019 mean trophic level β +0.06 (p = 0.107)
decision: Fail to reject H0 (no post-2015 improvement in the policy EEZs beyond the other SEA EEZs)
note: Five post-years (data end 2019) and few EEZs. Indonesia's ex-foreign vessels were mostly Indonesian-flagged, so Sea Around Us 'foreign' catch cannot show their removal (weak first stage). Sea Around Us reconstructions after ~2014 lean on national reports carried forward, so recent years are less independent. Vietnam's EU yellow card (Oct 2017) is in the Thai control group for 2018–2019. Stock status responds to fishing with a lag, so a short window can miss a real effect.

question: Do countries with a weaker response to illegal fishing, or more of it, have worse stock status?
evidence: Cross-country OLS, standardised, controls log GDP per capita and log catch, HC3 SEs, Holm over 6 tests. IUU response score (5 = weakest) → trophic-level trend (EPI RMTI): β_std +0.12 (n 139, Holm p = 1.000); IUU response score (5 = weakest) → median B/Bmsy (RAM): β_std -0.06 (n 19, Holm p = 1.000); IUU response score (5 = weakest) → % stocks above Umsy (RAM): β_std +0.20 (n 19, Holm p = 1.000); IUU prevalence score (5 = most) → trophic-level trend (EPI RMTI): β_std +0.10 (n 139, Holm p = 1.000); IUU prevalence score (5 = most) → median B/Bmsy (RAM): β_std +0.01 (n 19, Holm p = 1.000); IUU prevalence score (5 = most) → % stocks above Umsy (RAM): β_std +0.31 (n 19, Holm p = 1.000)
note: IUU index scores are expert/indicator composites for 2019 (152 coastal states); RMTI is a Sea Around Us trophic-level trend; RAM country values cover only countries with ≥ 3 assessed stocks (mostly high-income). Cross-section: association, not cause; richer countries both manage better and assess more.

question: Do countries paying more capacity-enhancing subsidies per tonne of catch have worse stock status?
evidence: Sumaila et al. 2019 (2018 subsidies, 152 countries), per tonne of 2018 capture, log(1 + USD/t); same controls and SEs, Holm over 6 tests. capacity-enhancing subsidy per t → trophic-level trend (EPI RMTI): β_std -0.13 (n 140, Holm p = 1.000); capacity-enhancing subsidy per t → median B/Bmsy (RAM): β_std -0.41 (n 19, Holm p = 1.000); capacity-enhancing subsidy per t → % stocks above Umsy (RAM): β_std +0.26 (n 19, Holm p = 1.000); beneficial subsidy per t → trophic-level trend (EPI RMTI): β_std -0.27 (n 140, Holm p = 0.013); beneficial subsidy per t → median B/Bmsy (RAM): β_std -0.13 (n 19, Holm p = 1.000); beneficial subsidy per t → % stocks above Umsy (RAM): β_std -0.21 (n 19, Holm p = 1.000)
decision: Fail to reject H0 (capacity-enhancing subsidies: 3 of 3 in the expected direction, none significant after Holm; beneficial subsidies go with a falling trophic level, the opposite of expected)
note: One year of subsidy data (2018); 'modeled' amounts are estimates where only evidence of a subsidy was found. Subsidies paid to distant-water fleets act on other countries' waters, which a per-country EEZ measure (RMTI) cannot see. Cross-section: association, not cause.

question: Reject H0 for both H1a and H1b?
evidence: H1a: Reject H0; H1b: Fail to reject H0
note: Stage 2 results are reported as exploratory/conditional

question: Reject H0 for both H1a and H1b (iteration 2: effort)?
evidence: H1a: Reject H0; H1b (iteration 2: effort): Fail to reject H0
note: Stage 2 results are reported as exploratory/conditional
